why_this_file_exists: The 2026-11-17 brief makes measurement the first job: 'Turn on click and conversion measurement before writing anything else', with a privacy-preserving outbound-click counter, a self-hosted analytics endpoint, five defined events, and an empty but well-defined campaign ledger. The brief also states the rule the ledger is built around: figures may be added 'only when obtained from authorized first-party reports'. This file is the contract — the event definitions, the collector's posture, the ledger schema and the deployment boundary. It contains no traffic data, because none exists yet.
what_this_is_not: This is not an analytics dashboard and it does not report a single measured reader. Every count on the measurement page is either zero, blank, or a number held in the reading device's own storage. Anyone who reads a number here as site-wide performance has misread the page, which is why the page says so in its first paragraph.

posture.what_runs: A click counter in the page's own script. It increments a tally in this browser's localStorage when a reader follows an outbound product link, and it notes which page the click came from. The measurement page reads the same tally back on request.
posture.what_does_not_run: No cookie is set. No fetch(), beacon, pixel, XHR or third-party script is called by the collector, so nothing leaves the reader's browser. No fingerprinting, no user or session identifier, no full destination query string, no IP address, and nothing is written to Amazon's Program Content.
posture.endpoint_status: not deployed — and it cannot be deployed on this host. GitHub Pages serves static files only, so there is nowhere for a browser to POST an event. The collector's endpoint constant is unset at build time, which is why the counter is local-only and why the ledger stays empty.
posture.deployment_boundary: Before any count on a reader's device can become a number about readers, four things have to exist: (1) a first-party endpoint on infrastructure the owner controls that accepts a POST and stores counts; (2) a retention and IP-handling policy for that endpoint, written down; (3) the privacy statement on this site updated from 'stored only on your device' to whatever the endpoint actually does, which is a Program Policies section 3(e) obligation and, for EU or UK readers, potentially a consent obligation; (4) a named person who reads the numbers. Until (1) exists, shipping the endpoint code would be a form with no mailbox.
posture.why_not_just_third_party: A hosted analytics script is the fast option and it is the one this project declines on its own evidence: section 3(e) requires an accurate statement of cookie and third-party technology use, the current notice says none are used, and a third-party script would make that sentence false the moment it loaded. The choice is not 'privacy vs measurement', it is 'which sentence the site has to rewrite'.

sources.used_for: Program Policies section 3(e) (cookie and third-party technology disclosure) and section 6(t)/2(b) (what Program Content may be used for)

events.name: outbound_click
events.definition: A reader activated a link on the affiliate host (a supplied product link, or a tagged Special Link once the tagging gate opens).
properties: page the click happened on (path only)
submitted-link id from the intent register (PI-01…PI-05) or 'other'
never_contains: the destination URL's query string, which carries Amazon-issued session and token parameters
anything Amazon serves as Program Content
events.decision_value: This is the only event that measures the thing an affiliate site is paid for, and the only one that can be counted honestly with no endpoint. A guide with zero outbound clicks on a product card is a card that is not doing its job, whichever way the traffic came.

events.name: cta_impression
events.definition: A product call-to-action block became visible in the reader's viewport, so that clicks have a denominator.
never_contains: scroll depth beyond the one threshold that fired the flag
events.decision_value: Clicks without impressions are a number with no unit. A 12-click month means nothing until you know whether 40 or 4,000 people saw the button; impression counts are what turn a click total into a click rate you can act on.

events.name: page_arrival
events.definition: A content page was opened in this browser, counted once per page per session-by-nothing (one increment per page view, no session concept at all).
properties: referring host only (not the full URL)
never_contains: full referrer URL, which can carry a search query the reader typed
events.decision_value: The topic calendar is currently argued, not measured — data/topics.json says so on its own face. Arrivals per page is the smallest dataset that could replace that argument, and it is the one number Search Console will also give the owner centrally, which is why this event is a cross-check and not the source of truth.

events.name: guide_reached_end
events.definition: A reader on an article page reached the article's closing block, which on this site is the 'read next' row rather than an ad load.
never_contains: time-based attention measurement, which is the version of this that reads as surveillance and is also the least reliable
events.decision_value: The brief asks for question-shaped guides and then asks whether anyone arrives. Arrival without completion cannot tell you whether the answer was useful; an article read to its end and never clicked is a different problem from an article abandoned at paragraph two, and the fix is different too.

events.name: first_party_report_row
events.definition: A dated row transcribed from a report the account holder is authorized to read: Associates earnings or Reports download for clicks, orders and units shipped per tracking ID.
never_contains: an estimate, modelled conversion rate or forecast in place of a report figure
a click total converted into a sales figure
any Amazon figure that is not in the owner's own report
events.status: not collected — no report access exists in this repository, so the ledger is empty by design
events.decision_value: This is the only event that can ever carry a conversion or revenue number, and it never comes from the browser: the click-to-order link is Amazon's to make, inside its own cookie window. A site-side 'conversion' count would be a guess wearing a decimal point.

ledger.purpose: The campaign ledger the brief asks for: empty, well-defined, and writable only from an authorized first-party report. It exists so that the first real number arrives in a row with provenance instead of in a sentence of prose that no one can check.

columns.label: Report date
columns.rule: The date the report covers, not the date it was read.

columns.label: Source
columns.rule: Named first-party report only, e.g. 'Associates Central › Reports › Earnings'. No third-party estimate, no scraped page, no modelled figure.

columns.label: Channel
columns.rule: The tracking ID or sub-tag the traffic is reported under, so a second channel later cannot be back-fitted into the first row.

columns.label: Eligible sessions
columns.rule: Blank unless the report states it. This site cannot measure a session.

columns.label: Clicks
columns.rule: The report's click count. The local browser counter is never summed into this column, and the build refuses a row that mixes them.

columns.label: Reported orders
columns.rule: Orders as reported by Amazon. Never clicks multiplied by an assumed rate.

columns.label: Transcribed on
columns.rule: The date a human copied the figure into this ledger. Two dates per row, so a stale row is visible as stale.

columns.label: Transcribed by
columns.rule: Who read the report. An automated agent may format the row; only an authorized human may supply the numbers.

ledger.why_empty: Nothing in this repository has Associates report access. The brief's own rule — add figures 'only when obtained from authorized first-party reports' — produces an empty table on the first day, and an empty table with a schema is the deliverable. Filling it from a browser counter or a forecast would be the exact failure the brief warns against.
first_row_checklist: Confirm the Associates account is past the 180-day three-qualifying-sales requirement (Q-03 is open on this).
Confirm which tracking ID the published links actually carry (Q-28, opened by this pass; the supplied ID shopnow047c-20 is recorded as owner-selected and unvalidated).
Make one sale, or wait for a report window, then download Reports › Earnings filtered to that tracking ID.
Add one row with all eight columns and rebuild. The build will accept the row; it will refuse a row with a blank source or a blank report date.

sub_tag_plan.what: Amazon's own tracking-ID mechanism already separates traffic sources without any script: extra tracking IDs on the same account each produce their own report, and the help page describes the pattern (storeid-20 with sub-IDs such as storeid-1-20). One ID per channel — site, newsletter, social — is measurement the site does not have to build, host or disclose a new technology for.
sub_tag_plan.limit: It attributes a channel, not a page. Clicks and orders arrive per tracking ID, not per URL, so a sub-tag plan answers 'which channel' and leaves 'which article' to EV-01/EV-03. S40 records a limit of 100 tracking IDs per associate account, so per-channel sub-tags are not a scarce resource at this site's scale.
sub_tag_plan.status: proposed; needs the account holder to create the IDs in Associates Central

sources.used_for: Tracking IDs and sub-tags: what they are, the storeid-20 / storeid-1-20 example, and where they are created
The screen where additional IDs are created, the 100-IDs-per-account limit, and the Tracking ID Summary Report where each ID's data is read — the report that answers Q-28

anti_patterns.name: Counting a click as a sale
anti_patterns.rule: A click total never becomes an order count, a conversion rate or an EPC. Only EV-05 may carry those, and only from a report.

anti_patterns.name: Publishing a dashboard nobody can source
anti_patterns.rule: Every number on a page of this site carries a source link or a stated reason it is blank. A chart of local browser counts is labelled as this device, or it does not ship.

anti_patterns.name: Measuring to look busy
anti_patterns.rule: Each event names the decision it informs. An event without one is removed rather than kept for completeness — that is how analytics sections rot into decoration.

anti_patterns.name: Trend theatre
anti_patterns.rule: No 'trending', 'popular' or 'most bought' label may be attached to a product on the strength of on-site counts. The evidence rule recorded in D-19 requires a dated snapshot from an official source for a popularity claim; five clicks in a browser's localStorage is not one.

verification.method: The policy obligations this design depends on were read live on 2026-11-17 in the same pass that re-read all five submitted links: Program Policies (section 3(e) cookie and technology disclosure; section 6(t) reviews and ratings; section 2(b) the Associates tag on links) and the tracking-ID help node, which is the source for the sub-tag pattern and for where tracking IDs are managed.
verification.what_is_not_verified: No claim here is verified against a live analytics system, because none is deployed. The counter's behaviour is verified the way any static-site behaviour is: the shipped script is checked by node --check, the events it writes are defined in this file, and the build refuses a page that claims a number this file does not contain.
